newsitem.title: POLAND: MOST GERMAN FIRMS IN POLAND WANT TO EXPAND.
newsitem.headline: MOST GERMAN FIRMS IN POLAND WANT TO EXPAND.

text.p: Most German entrepreneurs active in Poland aim to expand their businesses, primarily to take advantage of a 40-million-strong market, according to a survey released on Wednesday by a body promoting business ties.
The early 1996 survey showed that 70 percent of the German businesses polled wanted to expand, the Polish-German Association for Supporting the Economy said in a report.
The most commonly cited motive for setting up firms in Poland, mentioned by more than 7O percent of respondents, was the country's large domestic market.
Low labour costs were mentioned by around 35 percent, while about 25 percent mentioned Poland's association agreement with the European Union.
Asked what their principal market was, 59 percent said Poland, while most of those producing for export to Germany or the EU also wanted to build up sales domestically.
Almost half of German firms relied on materials from Germany, and 40 percent on local products, it said.
Germans disliked Polish bureaucracy and telephones.

"Clearly the instability of the legal framework and the functioning of the administration were assessed negatively," the report said, adding that common complaints were frequent changes in tax and customs rules, bureaucratic accounting regulations and customs procedures.
The report said 55 percent of German firms were happy with their results and four percent delighted, while 30 percent said they were below expectations and 11 percent were unhappy.
More than 75 percent saw the presence of German managers as essential to their ventures' success, although respondents praised Polish technical and engineering staff.
Polish workers were found to be more productive than workers in the former East Germany, but less efficient than in the former West Germany.
More than 90 percent said relations between Polish and German employees were good, 40 percent said they had become good through cooperation, while less than 10 percent described them as fair or bad.
The survey was among 340 German managers, mostly of firms in Warsaw, south and western Poland and border areas, of whom 115 responded, but only 103 replies were used in the results.
Most of the replies were from 100-percent German owned firms, and most companies were medium-sized.
Germany is second to the United States as a foreign investor, but official Polish figures do not show investments below $1 million which make up much German activity.
The association was founded by the two governments in 1994 and is owned by several German states and Polish provinces.
